title: Spray or Brush and Roll? How Pros Choose for Each Surface
description: Neither method is always better. Pros brush and roll most interior walls, spray cabinets, siding and brick, and use both on stucco, fences and decks. Here's what we use where, and why.
author: Chris Petkau
content:
Short answer: neither method is always better. It depends on the surface. In our work, we brush and roll most interior walls and trim, spray cabinets, siding and brick, and use both on stucco, fences and decks: we spray first, then back-roll or back-brush to work the coating into the surface. Spraying is faster to apply but needs much more masking. Brushing and rolling needs less setup and gives more control.

Spray vs. Brush and Roll at a Glance

  • Spraying: fastest application, smoothest finish on detailed surfaces, gets into texture and pores, but it needs full masking and has a risk of overspray

  • Brushing and rolling: little setup, precise edges and good control in occupied homes, but it's slower on large or detailed surfaces and can leave brush or roller marks if done poorly

What We Use on Each Surface

Interior walls and trim: brush and roll

Drywall is absorbent. Cutting in with a brush and rolling the walls pushes paint into the surface for even coverage and a consistent finish. With the right paint and long, smooth strokes, trim can be brushed without visible brush marks.

Ceilings: it depends on the size of the job

For a single room, we usually brush and roll. For a whole house where everything is being painted and masked anyway, an airless sprayer is faster. If we're painting only the ceiling, we roll it to keep overspray off the walls.

Cabinets, wainscoting and mantels: spray

For a smooth, factory-style finish with no brush or roller marks, we spray with a fine-finish tip. The room is sealed off with plastic, and floors, counters and everything not being painted are covered. It takes longer to set up, but that's how cabinets get that factory look. See our cabinet painting process.

Siding (Hardie board, fiber cement, vinyl): spray

Spraying covers each board and lap edge far faster and more evenly than brushing every row. On homes with unpainted brick next to the siding, which is common around Houston, we spray at low pressure with a narrow tip and mask carefully. Trim and soffits are finished with a brush. Learn more about fiber cement siding painting and vinyl siding painting.

Brick: spray

Brick is porous and full of nooks. Spraying gets paint into the mortar joints and pores that a roller would skip. See brick painting.

Stucco: both

We spray to get coating into the texture, then back-roll with a wet roller so the stucco fully absorbs it. That two-step approach gives better coverage and adhesion than either method alone. See stucco painting.

Fences and decks: both

Stain is sprayed on, then back-brushed so it soaks into the wood instead of sitting on top. See deck painting and staining.

Railings: it depends

Spindles are slow to brush one by one. If the house is already masked for spraying, railings get sprayed too. If overspray is a concern, we brush each spindle by hand. See railing painting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is spraying paint better than rolling?

Not automatically. Spraying gives a smoother finish on detailed surfaces like cabinets, but on interior walls a well-applied brush-and-roll finish is just as durable and needs far less masking.

Does spraying use more paint?

Usually yes. Some paint is lost as overspray, but the faster application often makes up for it on large or detailed surfaces.

Can you spray paint inside an occupied house?

Yes, with full masking and plastic barriers. For walls in lived-in rooms, brushing and rolling is usually more practical.
